sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Docker Compose describes a group of containers, networks, volumes, and runtime settings in one YAML file. It is useful for running a Go service with dependencies such as PostgreSQL or Redis as a repeatable local stack.

Compose creates a default network where services can reach each other by service name. `depends_on` controls creation order and can use health conditions in supported forms, but simple ordering alone does not prove that an application dependency is ready.

For example, an `api` service can use `DATABASE_URL=postgres://...@db:5432/app` and depend on a `db` service. Inside the network the hostname is `db`, not `localhost`, because localhost refers to the current container.

Compose does not make databases stateless or guarantee application readiness. Persistent data needs volumes, startup needs retries or health-aware conditions, and secrets and production availability need an explicit operational design.

Use Compose for local development, integration tests, demos, and small single-host setups where one command should reproduce the service topology. Keep production orchestration requirements separate unless Compose is deliberately the deployment tool.

sections.title: The core model: Docker Compose for a Go service
sections.content:
Docker Compose for a Go service is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

Compose turns a set of runtime commands into versioned application topology. A service definition selects an image or build, command, environment, ports, mounts, networks, and health settings. Containers on the same Compose network discover each other through service names, while published ports are needed only for access from outside that network. This distinction prevents a common error: the database is `db:5432` from the API container even if a different host port is published for a desktop client. Startup is a distributed-systems concern even on one laptop. A database process may have started before it can accept authenticated queries or before migrations complete. Health conditions can improve ordering, but the application should still handle temporary dependency failures according to its requirements. Named volumes preserve database files when containers are replaced. Bind mounts are useful for source code but can hide paths placed in an image, so their effect should be deliberate.

sections.title: Docker Compose for a Go service flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H[Host browser] -- published 8080 --> A[api:8080]
  A -- db:5432 on Compose network --> D[PostgreSQL]
  D --- V[(named volume)]
```

sections.title: Docker Compose for a Go service example
sections.content:
~~~yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: ${DATABASE_URL}
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
    volumes: ["db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
volumes:
  db-data: {}
~~~

sections.title: Docker Compose for a Go service at a glance
sections.content:
| Address used from | API address | Database address |
|---|---|---|
| Host machine | `localhost:8080` | Published host port, if configured |
| API container | Its own `localhost:8080` | `db:5432` |
| Database container | `api:8080` | Its own `localhost:5432` |
